items.title: ARRI’s Film Lab Adds 8mm, 16mm, and 65mm Film Looks With This Major Update
items.summary: While not a full step update (as in a version 1 to a version 2), this 1.5 version update for ARRI Film Lab is quite significant nonetheless. This major update to ARRI’s popular license-based OpenFX plugin should greatly expand its capabilities, bringing more creative options and parameters to filmmakers while improving processing speed and integration with your favorite color-managed workflows. Let’s check out what’s new in ARRI Film Lab 1.5 and how these new looks, grain control, and faster processing can enable smooth real-time 4K playback on your Apple Silicon MacBook Pro or other hardware. ARRI Film Lab Update 1.5 As mentioned above, this is a significant update from ARRI: Film Lab is set to add new looks alongside its 35mm option, plus new control over grain size and detail rendition. The license-based OpenFX plugin will also deliver up to four times faster processing, enabling smooth real-time 4K playback on Apple Silicon MacBook Pro systems and other hardware. The plugin will also offer a wider adjustment range, allowing stronger analog effects and further creative options, all of which, according to the company, come directly from user feedback. Perhaps the most significant update is the addition of new film format options; because the analog looks were previously based on 35mm film only, filmmakers can now choose 8mm, 16mm, or even 65mm as starting points. New Parameters and Anamorphic Ratio Control Other big updates include two new parameters (Grain Size and Rendition of Detail) that let you refine those choices further. Grain Size will help shooters adjust the scale of their grain, while Rendition of Detail changes perceived sharpness. Both offer a range of 0.75 to 1.5, helping users create looks that fall between each format's distinct aesthetics. This Film Lab 1.5 update will also introduce Anamorphic Ratio control, offering eight anamorphic squeeze ratios ranging from 1.25x to 2.0x. items.title: Movies Where the Hero Is Just an Ordinary Person
items.summary: Despite the conversation coming up every time a new film releases, we’re still very much in the superhero era of blockbuster entertainment. Believing in people with extraordinary abilities is still something very appealing to most people. But sometimes it’s fun to take a step back and appreciate when someone who saves the day isn’t a superpowered, benevolent billionaire. Here are some of the best movies where the hero is just a normal person. Alien 'Alien' Credit: 20th Century Fox Ridley Scott’s original 1979 masterpiece is about as chilling a piece of contained sci-fi horror that you can hope to find. The story is a tale as old as time, really. Put half a dozen or so people in a confined space, and let a big scary monster kill them all. Well, almost all of them. At the center of the film, of course, is iconic action heroine Ellen Ripley, played by Sigourney Weaver. Her portrayal of the character is so important to the modern monster movie that she even earned an Oscar nomination for her portrayal of the character in the film’s sequel, Aliens. While she is far from superpowered in that film, the far more claustrophobic, chamber piece-esque nature of the original film is what fully allows her everywoman persona to shine right through. She’s a natural leader; she’ll do whatever it takes to survive, and she beats the heck out of a mean AI robot. What’s not to love about Ellen Ripley? Die Hard 'Die Hard' Credit: Fox There are very few people out there that could play an action hero as nonchalantly and as ordinarily as Bruce Willis did during his iconic run of roles. As fantastic as performers as they were in their prime, there was always something about Schwarzenegger and Stallone that still felt somewhat physically unattainable. Willis, on the other hand, was in great shape, but you still felt like you could actually be put into the situations he found himself in. items.title: What It Took to Create the Costumes of Alexandra Byrne’s Elizabeth: The Golden Age
items.summary: Elizabeth: The Golden Age is an instructive case study in what period costume design actually costs and why. Working on a total production budget of approximately $55 million, director Shekhar Kapur and costume designer Alexandra Byrne faced the challenge of dressing an entire Elizabethan court authentically enough to serve a story about a queen whose public image was inseparable from what she wore. Byrne, who had previously designed the costumes for Kapur's Elizabeth (1998), won the Academy Award for Best Costume Design for her work on the sequel. Let’s dig into the extravagant spending behind making the 16th-century fabric used in Elizabeth: The Golden Age. Money Behind the Fabric One of the first calls any costume designer makes on a period production is whether to rent from existing stock or build from scratch. For Elizabeth: The Golden Age, renting was not viable. The film was shot at Shepperton Studios and on location across the U.K. The outdoor conditions would expose rented garments to mud, rain, and physical wear. Damage to rented period pieces carries steep replacement costs, and the logistics of cleaning and returning them mid-production add overhead that can quickly outpace the rental savings. Building new also gives the designer full creative control. According to Byrne, the fabric alone for a single Elizabeth gown cost approximately $3,000, before cutting, labor, embroidery, or accessories were factored in. What Made the 16th-Century Fabric So Expensive? These were expensive in the 16th century and remain expensive to reproduce. items.title: 10 Movies That Are Perfect for a Halloween Party
items.summary: It’s only natural to want to throw on a horror movie to play in the background during a Halloween party. However, it’s easy to accidentally throw off the vibe. Some horror movies are scary as you’re watching them, but don’t have the right visual atmosphere to augment the Halloween celebrations. Meanwhile, some have stories that are too engrossing that they’ll have people planted on the couch, fully watching the movie instead of mingling. These 10 movies avoid those problems, perfectly complementing the goings-on of a Halloween party with visual-forward approaches and stories that are either so familiar or segmented enough that they won’t necessarily drag attention away from the party for more than a few minutes at a time (AKA the perfect amount of time to divert attention when a conversation dries up). 10. Poltergeist (1982) Poltergeist has all the ghoulie ghosty vibes you need, and the plot is simple enough to understand if you’re dipping in and out. Carol Anne (Heather O'Rourke) has been abducted into the ghost realm, and her parents want to save her. What more do you need to know? What makes this a particularly strong pick for a Halloween party is that it is a very setpiece-focused horror film, so every few minutes there will be another firecracker of a horror scene that will provide an excellent backdrop for holiday celebrations. 9. Hausu (1977) Nobuhiko Obayashi’s surrealistic masterpiece Hausu is a visual feast. Every frame is full to the brim with exuberant, stylized imagery that turns even simple shots like a group of schoolgirls getting on a bus into an eerily scrumptious indulgence. The movie’s plot is also incredibly simple, essentially just presenting a series of scenes where the girls fall prey to a witch one by one. This isn’t a movie about plot. It’s a movie about experiencing the horror genre to its fullest extent. 8. The Beyond (1981) Lucio Fulci’s The Beyond is similar to Hausu in its irreverent approach to plot. items.title: 10 Essential Movies of 1988 Every Film Fan Should See
items.summary: The 1980s was an iconic decade for cinema, featuring many filmmakers working at the height of their powers, including John Hughes, Steven Spielberg, Amy Heckerling, and Rob Reiner. Even as they were winding down, there were still plenty of major titles produced that are well worth rewatching or checking out for the first time. To that end, we’re drilling deep on 1988 specifically to share 10 essential titles from that year. Without any further ado, let’s dive in! 10. License to Drive It’s important to remember that “essential” doesn’t mean “arthouse.” Understanding the teen culture of the 1980s is one of the most important things when trying to wrap one’s mind around the decade. And in 1988, outside of the Brat Pack, there was perhaps nobody more essential to teen culture than The Coreys. Just one year off from their first collaboration in the vampire movie The Lost Boys, Corey Haim and Corey Feldman reteamed for this charming “one crazy night” comedy about a teen trying not to let his lack of a driver’s license prevent him from impressing his date with a ride in a cool car. 9. My Neighbor Totoro The only reason why Hayao Miyazaki’s stunning anime masterwork My Neighbor Totoro is so low on this list is that, in the English-speaking world, it doesn’t “feel” like a 1988 movie. Its first English dub was released in 1989 exclusively on Japan Airlines flights, and it didn’t come to U.S. theaters until 1993, when said dub was put out by Troma Entertainment (yes, the company behind The Toxic Avenger). Regardless, it did debut in 1988, and it is essential in any era, bringing lovely, sweet magical realism to a deeply felt story about two sisters discovering spirits in the forest by their house, where they have recently moved to be closer to their hospitalized mother. 8. items.title: 6 Horror Movies To Watch for Hispanic Heritage Month
items.summary: From September 15 to October 15, National Hispanic Heritage Month in the United States celebrates and honors the culture and contributions of Hispanic Americans. Because the month brings us halfway into the Halloween season, this list will cover movies that are inspired by ghostly folklore, filmed in creepy stop-motion, or have monsters that are based on the dark history of South America. If you don’t know the Spanish language, don’t be afraid of the subtitles. Hearing the characters speak Spanish or the Mayan language will only pull you deeper into the culture and stories on-screen. Here is a diverse collection of different scares from different countries in six horror movies for Hispanic Heritage Month. Let’s get into them. The House That Screamed (1969) Country: Spain | Stream on Amazon Prime At a boarding school for troubled girls, a stifling environment is enforced by the iron-fist rule of headmistress Señora Fourneau (Lilli Palmer), with punishments and sexual repression filling the classrooms and corridors. Someone is bound to snap. ‘The House That Screamed’ (1969)Credit: Regia-Arturo González Rodríguez Director Narciso Ibáñez Serrador was famous for writing and directing the anthology horror TV series, Tales To Keep You Awake. In the first horror film that he directed, Serrador crafts a disquieting atmosphere in The House That Screamed with the location and cast. The school has beautiful, old architecture, with the corridors on the inside being shadowy and ornate. As the youths start to disappear, there are a few stylized kills that could mark this movie as a proto-slasher, but there is a greater focus on the abuse at the school. Unruly girls get lashings by fellow classmates who enjoy inflicting the pain. This is a Spanish Gothic horror classic where you won’t find ghosts. Humans are frightening on their own. items.title: Another Popular DJI Drone Set to Be Sunsetted as Support for the Phantom 4 Pro V2.0 to End Soon
items.summary: It’s always sad news when any camera or video product is sunsetted. Not only does it mean some popular gear that is likely still being used to create films, videos, or other projects is set to be retired, but it also just means we’re getting older. Let’s look at what we know about DJI's sunsetting announcement, a brief history of this popular aerial camera drone, and where aerial filmmakers, videographers, and cinematographers may want to look for replacement options. RIP to the DJI Phantom 4 Pro V2.0 One of DJI’s most popular and long-running aerial camera drone series, the Phantom line has a rich history of establishing the company as a major player in the space and, in effect, making aerial photography and videography a big business and a regular part of many filmmaking and video crews' workflows. The DJI Phantom 4 Pro V2.0 was a quadcopter drone with a powerful (at the time) 1-inch CMOS sensor, capable of shooting 4K/60fps video and 20MP photos, and it helped establish aerial cinematography as an art form unto itself. Officially listed on DJI’s “Notice of Suspension of Service and Support for Old Product Series” page, the Phantom 4 Pro V2.0 officially had its service suspended on October 31st, 2026. Production had already been suspended in August 2022, so it’s fair to say it had a good life and kept going for a while longer. Other Drone Options Sadly, if you are a DJI Phantom 4 Pro V2.0 owner or user looking for new options, many of the latest DJI drones aren't available in the US due to the ongoing drone ban and never-ending legal battle-slash-trade wars. If you’re looking for other drone options in the US, some new brands are on the scene, but the market isn’t nearly as robust as it used to be. So you may also want to look to second-hand markets or other ways to get DJI drones when abroad or through other means.

items.title: Film Quote of the Day: The Funniest Warning About John Wayne’s Gunslinger in 'Angel and the Badman'
items.summary: John Wayne has been in so many rugged Westerns that he became synonymous with gunfights and tense heroes. But the first Western he actually produced and starred in came with themes of pacifism and a lot of dry humor. That movie was James Edward Grant’s 1947 film Angel and the Badman. It's like this snappy dialogue movie that digs into the personalities of people we haven't seen in other westerns. You can see what drew Wayne to it and how much fun he had playing Quirt Evans. Today, I want to go over a line that's a warning about crossing the man, one that really pops off the screen and sells the signature tone. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com The Scene in Question In the film, Quirt Evans (John Wayne) is an infamous gunman who has been shot. That's a hazard of the job, and it leads him to a gentle Quaker family that takes him in and helps him mend. You get this simple opposites-attract story when he meets the daughter, Penelope Worth (Gail Russell). Penelope's kindness begins to melt Quirt’s hardened exterior, but his violent past refuses to let go so easily, and soon the people who gave him his gunshot wounds come calling. That's when we learn why Quirt became famous, and the family sees the other side of the man they've been watching over. During a tense moment where men consider confronting Quirt inside, we finally meet Laredo, the head of the gang of guys sent to kill Quirt. Laredo is no dummy, so when it comes time to ambush Quirt, one of his men says they should just bust in. That's when Laredo offers his men some advice. Hondo Jeffries: Hey, why don't we just bust in? Laredo Stevens: Because bustin' through doors with Quirt Evans on the other side ain't my idea of a healthy pastime. What The Quote Means Like I said at the top, this movie has a really experimental tone for Wayne. And this is a tongue-in-cheek look at how you can get yourself killed by a gunman in the Old West. items.title: A New 7-inch Cine Monitor is Here With an Ultra-Bright 2,800-Nit Display and Plenty of Connectivity
items.summary: Another new touchscreen cine monitor has arrived and, like the rest of the crowded market, it looks well-designed, capable of a wide range of uses, and packed with versatile connectivity. Can this new SWIT K7 stand out against its SmallHD, Atomos, and many other competitors? Let’s look at what this new 7-inch monitor offers: a bright FHD display, a rugged full-metal body with rubber corner protection, and 3G-SDI and HDMI 2.0 (4K60p) connectivity. The New SWIT K7 is Here While not SWIT's first cine monitor, the new K7 model suggests the company is doubling down on high-end, highly capable monitors for a wide range of pro-level productions, from on-location shoots to more stable studio setups. The SWIT K7 will likely stand out with its optically bonded 1920 x 1080 Full HD display, which should deliver a bright, clear image even in the brightest locations. The K7 will also feature a precision-CNC full-metal aluminum body with protective rubber corner guards that should help to ensure reliable protection on hectic sets and give filmmakers some nice peace of mind that any drops or smashes won’t ruin their shoots. The K7 is also set to offer a range of physical controls for tactile precision, including a scroll wheel for quick menu navigation, two customizable function keys, and a dedicated button that should let filmmakers instantly lock or unlock the touchscreen to prevent accidental inputs during critical takes. Connectivity and LUTs Another big selling point for this SWIT K7 is its 3G-SDI and HDMI 2.0 (4K60P) inputs and loop-out, plus SDI/HDMI cross-conversion to bridge different camera systems and external devices seamlessly. Filmmakers and video crews can also choose whether to apply the LUT to the SDI or HDMI output, helping send a graded signal to monitors that don't support internal LUTs.
